entries.title: [Correspondence] Governance reform in Eastern Mediterranean health systems
entries.description: Health systems in fragile and conflict-affected settings are often discussed in terms of what is broken—facilities, infrastructure, and financing. However, the real fracture line often runs through something less tangible and more foundational: governance. Recent publications on Syria's health system,1 the crisis in Gaza,2 and Africa's shifting health financing landscape,3 signal a deeper concern about the missing architecture for stewardship, legitimacy, and coordinated action. These are not simply health crises: they are crises of governance.

entries.title: Hubble spots a nearly invisible galaxy hiding in plain sight
entries.description: Hubble has captured the faint beauty of NGC 45, a spiral galaxy in Cetus whose glowing pink star-forming clouds reveal hidden activity. It belongs to the rare class of low surface brightness galaxies, dimmer than the night sky yet rich in gas and dark matter.

entries.title: The disappearing planet next door has astronomers intrigued
entries.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has detected strong evidence for a giant planet orbiting Alpha Centauri A, the nearest Sun-like star to Earth. Located just 4 light-years away, this possible Saturn-mass world may travel between one and two times the distance from its star that Earth does from the Sun. The planet appears to lie in the habitable zone, though its gas giant nature makes it unlikely to host life.

entries.title: AI finds hidden safe zones inside a fusion reactor
entries.description: Scientists have developed a lightning-fast AI tool called HEAT-ML that can spot hidden “safe zones” inside a fusion reactor where parts are protected from blistering plasma heat. Finding these areas, known as magnetic shadows, is key to keeping reactors running safely and moving fusion energy closer to reality.

entries.title: Twice a day, Mars may briefly host water that could support life
entries.description: Mars, once thought too cold and dry for liquid water, may briefly host salty brines twice a day during certain seasons. These fleeting bursts wouldn’t be enough to sustain humans, but they could have supported hardy life in Mars’ past—and may guide future missions searching for signs of it.

entries.title: Betelgeuse’s hidden companion star found after centuries of searching
entries.description: Astronomers have finally confirmed the existence of a long-suspected companion star orbiting Betelgeuse, the iconic red supergiant in Orion. Using the advanced 'Alopeke speckle imager on the Gemini North telescope, researchers overcame centuries of observational challenges to directly capture the elusive star.

entries.title: Voyager missed it, but now we know Uranus has a fiery secret
entries.description: For decades, scientists puzzled over why Uranus seemed colder than expected. Now, an international research team led by the University of Houston has solved the mystery: Uranus emits more heat than it gets from the Sun, meaning it still carries internal warmth from its ancient formation. This revelation rewrites what scientists know about the ice giant’s history, strengthens the case for NASA’s upcoming mission, and offers fresh insight into the forces shaping not only other planets, but also Earth’s future climate.

entries.title: What if dark matter came from a mirror universe?
entries.description: UC Santa Cruz physicist Stefano Profumo has put forward two imaginative but scientifically grounded theories that may help solve one of the biggest mysteries in physics: the origin of dark matter. In one, a hidden “mirror” universe with its own particles and forces could have created dense black hole–like objects in the early cosmos, making up all the dark matter we see today. The other theory suggests that dark matter might have been generated by quantum radiation at the universe’s edge during a rapid expansion shortly after the Big Bang.

entries.title: Strange spotted rock on Mars could reveal signs of ancient life
entries.description: A curious red Martian rock nicknamed Sapphire Canyon has scientists excited, as its spotted appearance hints at possible organic origins. On Earth, researchers tested a powerful laser technique, O-PTIR, on a similar rock found by chance in Arizona, proving it can rapidly and precisely reveal a material’s chemical makeup. This high-resolution method could play a key role in analyzing Mars samples once they arrive, adding to its growing track record in NASA missions like Europa Clipper.

entries.title: How scientists made quantum dots smarter and cheaper
entries.description: Researchers have found a clever way to make quantum dots, tiny light-emitting crystals, produce streams of perfectly controlled photons without relying on expensive, complex electronics. By using a precise sequence of laser pulses, the team can “tell” the quantum dots exactly how to emit light, making the process faster, cheaper, and more efficient. This advance could open the door to more practical quantum technologies, from ultra-secure communications to experiments that probe the limits of physics.
